quote: So my only, worry is that there so our panels are 440 watt panels.
stewart_read: Rep engages in a panel-count/wattage debate with the customer instead of using the escape hatch to defer to the specialist. This is accurate-but-premature content exactly matching the setter_scope_creep definition.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep might have been trying to build credibility by showing technical fluency, but the effect is a confusing exchange that doesn't resolve ('I think 28 panels for for us is high water wattage panels').
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to say 'that's exactly what our specialist will size for you on the call' instead of estimating panel counts live.

quote: Oh, yeah. I got that. But this guy told me that from Sunrise, there was gonna spent a great big beautiful bill next to them.
stewart_read: Customer discloses a specific prior Sunrun quote and a claim the competitor made about legislation, but the rep never asks what Sunrun actually quoted or offered — pure competitive intel left on the table.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have judged the legislative point was more urgent to correct than probing the competitor's pricing, but he doesn't ask a probing follow-up either way.
coaching_implication: Train a reflexive follow-up: 'What did Sunrun quote you?' any time a competitor name surfaces — free intel for the closer.

quote: And do you have a battery? ... But I definitely want a battery.
stewart_read: Customer volunteers strong interest in a battery add-on without being prompted — a clear signal of a larger potential deal (Tesla Powerwall).
coaching_implication: Rep should flag this explicitly for the closer in the handoff and reflect the interest back to the customer ('Great, we'll make sure the specialist speaks to Powerwall options') rather than just logging it flatly.

quote: My mom passed away. We're having a funeral on May 2, so it's gonna have to be after that.
stewart_read: The rep's response ('Okay. After the second. Alright. I'm sorry to hear that, by the way.') is a brief courtesy but immediately pivots back to scheduling logistics without pausing on the disclosure.
alternative_hypothesis: A short acknowledgment before returning to logistics is arguably appropriate pacing for a stranger on a sales call; over-dwelling could feel intrusive.
coaching_implication: A slightly longer, specific acknowledgment (pause, then 'take the time you need, we'll work around it') would land as more genuine before resuming scheduling.

quote: I see you have there is one tree in the backyard that looks like it shed you quite a bit. Is that tree still there? It doesn't shade as much.
stewart_read: This exchange is garbled in the transcript (likely cross-talk/mis-attribution) but the substantive content — asking about a tree affecting shading — is a legitimate roof/site verify item the rep does cover.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the diarization warning, the customer line may actually belong partly to the rep; treat the exact attribution with caution rather than coaching on it directly.
coaching_implication: No direct coaching action; flag to QA that this segment's speaker labels look unreliable if reviewing audio.

stewart_read: Rep visibly loses track of the customer's tax-credit/legislation question and has to ask them to repeat it, indicating uncertainty on a topic the customer raised confidently.
alternative_hypothesis: Could be simple audio/line static rather than a substantive knowledge gap, but the surrounding answer ('Yeah. No. That the bill that passed...') remains garbled and unclear regardless.
coaching_implication: If the rep doesn't have a clean, confident answer on tax-credit legislation, the escape hatch is better than an unclear answer: 'That's a great question for the specialist — they stay current on the latest state and federal incentives.'

quote: Yeah. He'll just come over and show you, like, the estimate and show you our numbers.
stewart_read: The rep sets a day/time (Friday the 8th at noon) but the button-up is thin — no one-hour block statement, no no-driving/computer instruction, no explicit 'is that fair' handshake beyond the customer's own 'we got an hour.'
alternative_hypothesis: The customer volunteering 'we got an hour' could be read as the customer self-supplying the block, reducing the need for the rep to restate it, but the rep never confirms computer/no-driving conditions at all.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to always run the full button-up checklist (hour block, no driving/at computer, 'is that fair') regardless of what the customer volunteers, since it's the rep's job to lock the mechanics, not assume the customer covered it.
